if a natural monopoly truly is a natural monopoly it will require government regulation to prevent it from extracting rents from the market and causing dead weight losses.

if it is not really a natural monopoly and faces a theoretical entry of a competitor into the market then the threat or the reality of a new entrant in the market will force the monopoly to keep costs and profit margins reasonable while providing services that the market values. if a monopoly is incompetent and inefficient, or sets prices too high, they will invite a competitor to enter the market because it is profitable and attractive.

so the real test of a monopoly is the barriers to entry to the market. if they are relatively low, the monopoly will be forced to set prices low to discourage competition or soon it will not be a monopoly anymore. If barriers to entry are very high monopolies have much more power and freedom to exploit their customers and the market and thus they require increased regulation to maintain efficiency

To add on to lasercow's excellent insight: This is why GOVERNMENT facilitated monopolies are dangerous, they usually arise through lobbying efforts and/or government sponsored barriers to entry - or the like. However, natural monopolies usually offer consumers a better products, lower prices, or even appeal to consumers' humanitarian side - because they are always in constant competition with lasercows's mention of the "theoretical entry of a competitor into the market."

depends...government facilitated monopolies can displace other less efficient monopolistic market structures. It depends on the motive and function of the government intervention.

But, government intervention in markets is dangerous, because it is rarely done with a full understanding of the cost benefit analysis and risk of unintended consequences....but more MUCH more importantly, because it is a corruptible institution, which does not face real market pressures itself, and thus it is widely used by, powerful groups of all kinds, to extract value from humankind and cause tremendous dead-weight losses....at the cost of human livelihood and future prosperity and survival.

The typical solution is contract bidding.

A city only needs one water company, but the govt. gets to choose who to award the contract to. A regulatory agency sets standards for quality, then every firm competing for the bid has an incentive to trim all the fat they can. If the natural monopoly increases their rates for no reason then when the contract is up another company will be able to undercut them. I think rates are also negotiated during that bidding process, but I am not positive.

Then of course govt has the option to regulate all kinds of variables along the way.

Terry Fox runs in his blood stained shorts, during his Marathon of Hope run across Canada in July 1980. He ran a marathon a day for 143 days before succumbing to his cancer.

TerryFox (July 28, 1958 – June 28, 1981) was Canadian who in 1980, with one leg having been amputated, embarked on a cross-Canada run to raise money and awareness for cancer research. Although the spread of his cancer eventually forced him to end his quest after 143 days and 5,373 kilometres (3,339 mi), and ultimately cost him his life, his efforts resulted in a lasting, worldwide legacy. The annual Terry Fox Run, has grown to involve millions of participants in over 60 countries and is now the world's largest one-day fundraiser for cancer research; over C$600 million has been raised in his name, Source
